$comment: Learn entries in one language (PHASE4_SPEC 3.2). Keys are registry ids. English is the source language; other languages translate it.

rope_mainsheet.name: Mainsheet
rope_mainsheet.short: The rope that lets the boom and mainsail swing out, or pulls them back in.
rope_mainsheet.what: Easing (letting out) the mainsheet lets the wind push the boom further out; hauling it in pulls the boom back towards the middle. The rope only limits how far the boom can go: with the wind from ahead, easing it just makes it slack. Near the middle a little rope moves the boom a lot; far out, a lot of rope moves it only a little.
rope_mainsheet.onThisBoat: A German mainsheet: one rope with two ends, one at each side of the cockpit (the clutches say “Main sheet” and “MAIN SHEET”). It runs through three blocks under the boom and two spring-mounted blocks at the back of the coachroof. There is no traveller (a sliding car for the lower blocks).

mistakes.mistake: Easing it far more than the wind needs.
mistakes.fix: The mainsail flaps along its front edge. Haul in until the flapping just stops.

mistakes.mistake: Keeping it hauled hard in a gust.
mistakes.fix: The boat heels a lot and turns into the wind by herself. Ease the mainsheet to let the gust out.

mistakes.mistake: Opening its clutch under load with the rope not on a winch.
mistakes.fix: The rope runs out fast and the boom flies out. Put the rope on the winch first, then open the clutch.

rope_mainsheet.showMe: Wind from the side and the mainsheet eased to 60 %: the boom has swung well out. Tap “Mainsheet” below and haul it in: the boom comes back towards the middle.

rope_jib_sheet.name: Jib sheet
rope_jib_sheet.short: The rope that sets how far the jib can swing out.
rope_jib_sheet.what: Hauling the jib sheet in pulls the jib’s back corner towards the boat; easing it lets the wind push the jib out. On a self-tacking jib, easing mostly lets the top of the sail twist open rather than swinging the whole sail out.
rope_jib_sheet.onThisBoat: One sheet runs from the jib’s back corner to a car on a short track in front of the mast, with a 2:1 purchase (a pulley system that halves the pull), then down the mast and aft to the starboard clutches. The clutch says “Genoa sheet”, but the sail is a jib. Fully eased, the jib only reaches about 30° out.

mistakes.mistake: Easing it on a reach and expecting the jib to swing far out.
mistakes.fix: A self-tacking jib cannot go far out; easing more only twists its top open. Ease until its telltales stream, no further.

mistakes.mistake: Furling the jib with the sheet still tight.
mistakes.fix: The jib stops rolling up. Ease the jib sheet first, then pull the furling line.

mistakes.mistake: Hauling it hard in with the wind from the side.
mistakes.fix: The jib stalls: the telltales on its far side droop. Ease until they stream.

rope_jib_sheet.showMe: Wind from the side and the jib sheet fully eased: the jib is only about 30° out, but its top has twisted open. Tap “Jib sheet” below and haul it in to see the jib flatten.

rope_vang.name: Vang
rope_vang.short: Pulls the boom down, which keeps the mainsail flatter and stops its top twisting open.
rope_vang.what: The vang runs from low on the mast to the underside of the boom. Hauled, it holds the boom down, so the sail stays flatter with less twist. Eased, the boom end rises and the top of the sail twists open. Once the mainsheet is eased well out, the vang, not the sheet, decides how high the boom sits.
rope_vang.onThisBoat: A rigid vang (a strut with a gas spring inside) with a rope tackle. The spring holds the boom up, so the boom does not drop when the vang is eased; the rope only pulls it down. Its clutch is on the port side, labelled “Vang”.

mistakes.mistake: Relying on the mainsheet to hold the boom down on a reach.
mistakes.fix: Far out, the sheet pulls sideways, not down, and the boom lifts. Haul the vang to hold it down.

mistakes.mistake: Hauling the vang and the topping lift tight at the same time.
mistakes.fix: They pull against each other (both ropes turn red in the app). Ease the topping lift once the sail is set.

rope_vang.showMe: Wind 20 kn from the side, vang eased all the way: the boom end has lifted and the top of the mainsail twists open. Tap “Vang” below and haul it in: the boom comes down and the sail flattens.

rope_topping_lift.name: Topping lift
rope_topping_lift.short: A line from the top of the mast to the end of the boom that can hold the boom up.
rope_topping_lift.what: The topping lift carries the boom when the sail is not holding it up, for example with the sail rolled away. Hauled tight while sailing, it fights the vang and spoils the sail’s shape, so it is eased once the sail is set.
rope_topping_lift.onThisBoat: Labelled “Boom lift” on the port clutches. The rigid vang’s spring already holds the boom up, so on this boat the topping lift only carries the boom when it is hauled higher than the spring holds it.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving it tight while sailing with the vang hauled.
mistakes.fix: The two ropes fight (both turn red in the app). Ease the topping lift.

rope_topping_lift.showMe: No wind, the topping lift and the vang both hauled tight: they pull against each other and both ropes turn red. Tap “Topping lift” below and ease it to end the fight.

rope_outhaul.name: Outhaul
rope_outhaul.short: Pulls the mainsail’s back bottom corner (the clew) out along the boom.
rope_outhaul.what: The outhaul pulls the clew towards the end of the boom. With in-mast furling it also pulls the sail out of the mast as it unrolls: it is hauled together with the furling line’s “out” tail, and eased when the sail is rolled in.
rope_outhaul.onThisBoat: Labelled “Main outhaul” on the port clutches. In the app’s Easy mode it moves together with “Mainsail out”. How the rope runs inside the boom is not yet confirmed on the real boat.

mistakes.mistake: Rolling the main in without easing the outhaul.
mistakes.fix: The outhaul holds the clew out and the sail cannot roll in. Ease the outhaul as you pull the “in” furling line.

mistakes.mistake: Unrolling the main without hauling the outhaul.
mistakes.fix: The sail comes out baggy and does not reach the end of the boom. Haul the outhaul together with the “out” line.

rope_outhaul.showMe: Mainsail fully out: the outhaul holds its back corner at the end of the boom. Tap “Outhaul” below and roll the main in a little: the corner slides towards the mast.

rope_main_furling_line.name: Main furling line
rope_main_furling_line.short: Rolls the mainsail into the mast, or lets it out.
rope_main_furling_line.what: In-mast furling rolls the mainsail up inside the mast like a blind. The furling line has two tails: hauling the “in” tail rolls the sail in; hauling the “out” tail, together with the outhaul, rolls it out while the “in” tail is eased. Rolling the sail partly in makes it smaller in strong wind (instead of reefing).
rope_main_furling_line.onThisBoat: Two clutches on the starboard side, both labelled “Main furling”: the left one rolls the main in, the right one rolls it out. If the line slips, the main can be rolled in by hand with the winch handle in the gearbox at the foot of the mast (about 40 turns).

mistakes.mistake: Hauling the “in” tail without easing the “out” tail and the outhaul.
mistakes.fix: Nothing moves, or the line jams. Ease the other two first.

mistakes.mistake: Rolling the main in while it is full of wind.
mistakes.fix: The load is heavy and the line can slip. Ease the mainsheet, or turn closer to the wind, so the sail is not pulling, then roll it in.

rope_main_furling_line.showMe: Mainsail 30 % out: most of it is rolled inside the mast. Tap “Main furling line” below and set “Mainsail out” to 100 % to unroll it.

rope_jib_furling_line.name: Jib furling line
rope_jib_furling_line.short: Rolls the jib up round the forestay, or lets it unroll.
rope_jib_furling_line.what: Pulling the line turns the drum at the bottom of the forestay and rolls the jib up around it. Easing it while pulling the sheet lets the jib unroll. A partly rolled jib is smaller, which helps in strong wind.
rope_jib_furling_line.onThisBoat: A Furlex furler at the bow. The line runs back along the port side deck through a single clutch labelled “JIB ROLL” to the port winch. The jib sheet must be eased for the jib to roll up.

mistakes.mistake: Pulling the furling line with the jib sheet tight.
mistakes.fix: The jib stops rolling. Ease the jib sheet, then keep furling.

mistakes.mistake: Letting the line run free when unrolling in strong wind.
mistakes.fix: The jib flies out and flaps hard. Keep a turn of the line on the winch and let it out under control.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving the jib flapping for a long time in strong wind.
mistakes.fix: The sail wears and can tear. Roll it in or sheet it in quickly.

rope_jib_furling_line.showMe: Jib 40 % out with its sheet eased: the rest is rolled round the forestay. Tap “Jib furling line” below and change “Jib out” to roll it in or out.

rope_main_halyard.name: Main halyard
rope_main_halyard.short: Holds the top of the mainsail up the mast.
rope_main_halyard.what: A halyard hoists a sail. The main halyard holds the mainsail’s top corner (the head) at the top of the mast.
rope_main_halyard.onThisBoat: With in-mast furling the sail stays hoisted inside the mast; it is rolled in and out instead of being lowered. The halyard’s clutch on the starboard side (“Main halyard”) normally stays shut. The app does not adjust it.

mistakes.mistake: Opening the main halyard clutch by mistake (it sits next to the sheets).
mistakes.fix: The sail’s head can slide down inside the mast. Leave this clutch shut, and read the label before opening any clutch.

rope_spi_halyard.name: Gennaker halyard
rope_spi_halyard.short: The halyard for a gennaker; on this boat it is kept parked.
rope_spi_halyard.what: A halyard for hoisting a gennaker (a large, light sail for wind from behind) to the top of the mast.
rope_spi_halyard.onThisBoat: The boat has no gennaker on board, but the halyard is fitted; its clutch on the port side is labelled “SPI HALYARD”. The app draws its top end parked down the front of the mast (where it is really kept is not yet known).

mistakes.mistake: Leaving the parked halyard loose.
mistakes.fix: It slaps against the mast and can wrap round the forestay or the jib. Keep it parked and tight.

part_hull.name: Hull
part_hull.short: The body of the boat, which floats.
part_hull.what: The hull is the watertight body that floats and carries everything else. Its shape under the water decides how easily she moves and how far she leans.
part_hull.onThisBoat: 15.55 m long overall, 4.75 m wide, 13.54 m on the waterline, and about 14.7 tonnes empty.

part_bow.name: Bow
part_bow.what: The bow is the front end of the boat. Directions on board are given from it: ahead is in front of the bow.
part_bow.onThisBoat: The jib furler, the anchor roller and the anchor windlass sit on the bow.

part_stern.name: Stern
part_stern.what: The stern is the back end of the boat. Astern means behind it.
part_stern.onThisBoat: A wide, flat stern; the two wheels stand just in front of it.

part_deck.name: Deck
part_deck.short: The top of the hull that you walk on.
part_deck.what: The deck closes the hull from above. Ropes, blocks and fittings are fixed to it, and the crew walks along it to go forward.
part_deck.onThisBoat: The side decks run from the cockpit to the bow on each side of the coachroof.

part_coachroof.name: Coachroof
part_coachroof.short: The raised roof over the cabin, between the mast and the cockpit.
part_coachroof.what: The coachroof raises the deck over the living space below to give headroom. Ropes from the mast run aft over it to the cockpit.
part_coachroof.onThisBoat: The mast stands on it. The mainsheet’s two deck blocks sit at its back end, and covered channels carry the ropes from the foot of the mast to the clutches.

part_cockpit.name: Cockpit
part_cockpit.short: The open, sunken area at the back where the crew sits and steers.
part_cockpit.what: The cockpit is where the crew sits, steers and works most of the ropes. It lies lower than the deck, so it feels safer at sea.
part_cockpit.onThisBoat: Two wheels at the back, one winch and one clutch bank on each side, the engine lever at the helm, and the instruments and the autopilot control by the wheels.

part_companionway.name: Companionway
part_companionway.short: The entrance with steps from the cockpit down into the cabin.
part_companionway.what: The companionway is the hatch and steps that lead below.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving it open when waves start coming aboard.
mistakes.fix: Water can pour below. Close it in rough weather.

part_keel.name: Keel
part_keel.short: The heavy fin under the boat that stops her sliding sideways and keeps her upright.
part_keel.what: The keel does two jobs. Moving through the water, it works like a wing and stops the wind pushing the boat sideways, so she can sail across and towards the wind. Its weight, low down, pulls her back upright when the wind heels her.
part_keel.onThisBoat: An L-shaped keel 2.40 m deep (a shorter 1.98 m keel is an option) with a 4-tonne ballast bulb at the bottom.

part_rudder.name: Rudder
part_rudder.short: The blade under the back of the boat that steers her.
part_rudder.what: Turning the wheel turns the rudder. The water flowing past it pushes the stern sideways, and the boat turns. With no speed through the water there is no flow, so the rudder does nothing.
part_rudder.onThisBoat: One rudder, turned by either of the two wheels; an emergency tiller can be fitted if the steering fails. In the app the wheel turns the rudder up to 35° each way.

mistakes.mistake: Turning the wheel hard over while the boat is stopped.
mistakes.fix: Nothing happens: the rudder needs water flowing past it. Get her moving first, with the sails or the engine.

mistakes.mistake: Turning the wheel further and further against a boat that turns into the wind in a gust.
mistakes.fix: A rudder turned too far stops gripping. Ease the mainsheet instead, so she stops turning.

part_rudder.showMe: The wheel is turned 25° to starboard: look through the water under the stern to see the rudder blade turned. Under way, this turns the boat to starboard.

part_saildrive.name: Saildrive and propeller
part_saildrive.short: The engine’s drive leg and propeller under the hull.
part_saildrive.what: A saildrive is a leg that comes down through the bottom of the hull from the engine, with the propeller on its end. It pushes the boat ahead or astern when the engine is in gear.
part_saildrive.onThisBoat: A diesel engine of about 80 hp, a saildrive and a fixed two-blade propeller. In the app, full throttle (2,500 rpm) gives about 9.3 kn.

mistakes.mistake: Putting the engine in gear with a rope in the water near the stern.
mistakes.fix: The propeller can catch the rope and stop the engine. Get all ropes on board before you engage gear.

part_lifelines.name: Lifelines and stanchions
part_lifelines.short: The wires round the edge of the deck, held up by posts.
part_lifelines.what: Lifelines are wires along the edge of the deck, held up by posts (stanchions). They help stop people falling overboard, but they are low: hold on to the boat as well.

mistakes.mistake: Leaning or sitting with your weight on the lifelines.
mistakes.fix: They can bend or give way. Hold on to something solid and keep your weight inside the boat.

env_water.name: Water surface
env_water.short: The sea around the boat; its waves grow with the wind.
env_water.what: Waves grow with the wind’s strength and with the distance it blows over open water. The boat rises and falls, pitches and rolls on them; waves from ahead slow her, waves from behind at an angle push her off course. In the app the water is see-through, so the keel and rudder stay visible.
env_water.showMe: Open sea in 20 kn of wind from the side: waves about 2 m high roll the boat. Change “Waves” in Conditions to compare.

part_mast.name: Mast
part_mast.short: The tall pole that holds the sails up.
part_mast.what: The mast holds up the sails. Wires (the standing rigging) hold it in place from the sides, the front and the back.
part_mast.onThisBoat: A Seldén aluminium mast standing on the coachroof, its top about 22 m above the water, with two sets of swept-back spreaders. The mainsail rolls up inside it.

part_boom.name: Boom
part_boom.short: The pole along the bottom of the mainsail.
part_boom.what: The boom holds the bottom of the mainsail out from the mast. It swings across the boat when the wind changes side; the mainsheet, the vang and the topping lift set where it sits.
part_boom.onThisBoat: 6.25 m long, joined to the mast by the gooseneck. It can swing about 72° out to each side before it would touch the shrouds.

mistakes.mistake: Standing or sitting in the boom’s path with the wind from behind.
mistakes.fix: In an accidental gybe the boom crosses the boat fast and hard. Keep your head out of the red danger zone the app draws.

part_boom.showMe: Wind from the side: the boom has swung out to the side away from the wind. Try “Mainsheet” or “Vang” below to see it move.

part_gooseneck.name: Gooseneck
part_gooseneck.short: The joint between the boom and the mast.
part_gooseneck.what: The gooseneck lets the boom swing from side to side and tilt up and down.

part_spreader.name: Spreaders
part_spreader.short: Short struts out from the sides of the mast that spread the shrouds.
part_spreader.what: Spreaders push the shrouds out from the mast, so the wires hold it at a better angle.
part_spreader.onThisBoat: Two sets, about 6 m and 12 m above the foot of the mast, swept back 24°. With the boom far out, the mainsail presses against them.

part_shroud.name: Shrouds
part_shroud.short: The wires that hold the mast up from the sides.
part_shroud.what: Shrouds run from the mast down to each side of the deck. They stop the mast falling sideways and take much of the sails’ load.
part_shroud.onThisBoat: The outer shrouds stop the boom at about 72° out.

part_forestay.name: Forestay
part_forestay.short: The wire from high on the mast to the bow; the jib is set on it.
part_forestay.what: The forestay holds the mast from the front. The jib’s front edge runs along it, and the furler rolls the jib up round it.
part_forestay.onThisBoat: One forestay, with the Furlex jib furler at its foot.

part_backstay.name: Backstay
part_backstay.short: The wire from the top of the mast to the stern.
part_backstay.what: The backstay holds the mast from behind, against the pull of the forestay and the jib.

env_wind.name: Wind
env_wind.short: The air moving over the water; in the app you set it in Conditions.
env_wind.what: The wind is described by where it comes from and by its speed in knots. The streaks in the 3D view show it. Conditions sets its direction (from 0° north, clockwise) and speed, and can make it gusty, shifty, building or dying.

mistakes.mistake: Reading a wind direction as where the wind blows to.
mistakes.fix: A wind “from 060°” blows from the east-north-east towards the west-south-west.

env_wind.showMe: Wind 12 kn from 060°: the streaks show it blowing past the boat. Turn the dial in Conditions to change it.

part_windex.name: Masthead wind indicator

alternatives.note: a brand name, used for any such indicator

part_windex.short: The little arrow at the top of the mast that shows where the wind comes from.
part_windex.what: It turns like a weathervane and points into the wind the boat feels (the apparent wind). Look up at it to check the wind’s angle.

part_main_furling_gearbox.name: In-mast furling gearbox
part_main_furling_gearbox.short: The gearbox at the foot of the mast that turns the mainsail’s furling rod.
part_main_furling_gearbox.what: The furling line turns a drum on this gearbox, which turns a rod inside the mast and rolls the sail in or out. A socket for the winch handle lets you roll the sail by hand.
part_main_furling_gearbox.onThisBoat: A Seldén gearbox with an IN/OUT switch (IN to the left, OUT to the right). With the winch handle, about 40 turns roll the main in. In Realistic mode it is at the Mast station.

mistakes.mistake: Cranking with the switch on OUT when you want to roll the main in.
mistakes.fix: The sail comes further out. Set the switch to IN first.

part_main_furling_gearbox.showMe: Realistic mode, Mast station: the gearbox with its IN/OUT switch and the socket for the winch handle.

part_jib_furler.name: Jib furler

alternatives.note: the maker’s name for this furler

part_jib_furler.short: The drum and swivel on the forestay that roll the jib up.
part_jib_furler.what: Pulling the furling line turns the drum at the bottom of the forestay, and the jib rolls up round the stay like a blind. It can stop part way, to make the jib smaller.
part_jib_furler.onThisBoat: A Seldén Furlex 404S at the bow. Its line runs aft along the port side deck to the “JIB ROLL” clutch.
part_jib_furler.showMe: Jib 40 % out: the rest is rolled round the forestay, above the furler’s drum.

sail_main.name: Mainsail
sail_main.short: The sail behind the mast, held by the mast and the boom.
sail_main.what: The mainsail is set on the mast and the boom. The mainsheet sets its angle to the wind, the vang its twist, and the outhaul pulls it out along the boom. Trimmed right, it drives the boat; pulled in too far it stalls, let out too far it flaps.
sail_main.onThisBoat: 61 m², rolled into the mast (in-mast furling), with no battens (stiffening strips). In strong wind it is made smaller by rolling part of it into the mast.

mistakes.mistake: Pulling it in too far for the wind angle.
mistakes.fix: It stalls: less drive and more heel, and the telltales on its far side droop. Ease until they stream.

mistakes.mistake: Letting it out too far.
mistakes.fix: Its front edge flaps. Haul in until the flapping just stops.

mistakes.mistake: Keeping all of it out as the wind gets strong.
mistakes.fix: The boat heels too much and turns into the wind by herself. Roll part of it in.

sail_main.showMe: Sailing 60° off the wind with the mainsail trimmed well: its telltales stream and it drives the boat at about 7 kn. Tap “Mainsheet” below and ease it fully: the front edge starts to flap and she slows down.

sail_jib.name: Self-tacking jib
sail_jib.short: The front sail; it changes sides by itself when the boat tacks.
sail_jib.what: The jib is set on the forestay in front of the mast. Its sheet runs to a car on a track across the deck, and the car slides to the other side by itself when the bow turns through the wind, so tacking needs no sheet work.
sail_jib.onThisBoat: 51.5 m², on a Furlex roller furler at the bow. The track is short and straight, so the jib cannot be eased far out: fully eased it reaches about 30°. The clutch says “Genoa sheet”, but the sail is a jib, smaller than a genoa and not overlapping the mast.

mistakes.mistake: Keeping all of the jib out in strong wind.
mistakes.fix: She heels too much and turns into the wind. Roll part of the main in first, then part of the jib if needed.

mistakes.mistake: Furling the jib with the sheet tight.
mistakes.fix: Ease the sheet; then the jib rolls up.

sail_jib.showMe: Wind 30° from starboard: the jib’s car sits at the port end of its track. In Conditions, turn the wind to the other side of the bow: the car slides across by itself.

sail_gennaker.name: Gennaker
sail_gennaker.short: A large, light sail for wind from behind; not on board this boat.
sail_gennaker.what: A gennaker is a big, light, curved sail flown from the bow and the top of the mast when the wind comes from behind the side. It is set and taken down for each use.
sail_gennaker.onThisBoat: Not on the reference boat; only its halyard (“SPI HALYARD”) is fitted. The manual gives 200 m² for the optional gennaker. The app does not show the sail.

sailpart_head.name: Head
sailpart_head.short: The top corner of a sail.
sailpart_head.what: The head is the corner the halyard pulls up.
sailpart_head.onThisBoat: The mainsail’s head stays at the top of the mast, inside the furling slot; the jib’s head is at the top of the forestay.

sailpart_tack.name: Tack (corner)
sailpart_tack.short: The front bottom corner of a sail.
sailpart_tack.what: The tack is fixed at the front bottom of the sail: the mainsail’s at the gooseneck (where the boom meets the mast), the jib’s at the furler drum on the bow. “Tack” also means turning the bow through the wind, and the side the wind comes from: see “Tacking” and “Starboard tack”.

sailpart_clew.name: Clew
sailpart_clew.short: The back bottom corner of a sail, where the sheet pulls.
sailpart_clew.what: The sheet pulls on the clew and so sets the sail’s angle to the wind. On the mainsail the outhaul also pulls the clew along the boom.
sailpart_clew.onThisBoat: When the mainsail is rolled in, its clew moves along the boom to the mast; when the jib is rolled in, its clew moves forward round the forestay.

sailpart_luff.name: Luff
sailpart_luff.short: The front edge of a sail.
sailpart_luff.what: The wind meets the sail at the luff. When a sail is let out too far, the luff starts to flap first: that is “luffing”.
sailpart_luff.onThisBoat: The mainsail’s luff runs up inside the mast’s furling slot; the jib’s runs along the forestay.

sailpart_leech.name: Leech
sailpart_leech.short: The back edge of a sail.
sailpart_leech.what: The wind leaves the sail at the leech. Twist is how much the top of the leech falls away to the side; the vang controls it on the mainsail, the sheet on the jib.

sailpart_foot.name: Foot
sailpart_foot.short: The bottom edge of a sail.
sailpart_foot.what: The foot runs from the tack to the clew. The mainsail’s foot runs along the boom, and the outhaul stretches it.

fit_mainsheet_boom_blocks.name: Mainsheet blocks on the boom
fit_mainsheet_boom_blocks.short: The three pulleys under the boom that the mainsheet runs through.
fit_mainsheet_boom_blocks.what: The mainsheet runs back and forth between these blocks and the deck blocks. Each extra part of rope makes it easier to pull (more purchase).
fit_mainsheet_boom_blocks.onThisBoat: Three blocks under the boom, 2.9 m from the mast.

fit_mainsheet_deck_blocks.name: Mainsheet deck blocks
fit_mainsheet_deck_blocks.short: The two spring-mounted pulleys at the back of the coachroof for the mainsheet.
fit_mainsheet_deck_blocks.what: Each end of the mainsheet comes down from the boom to one of these blocks. The springs keep the blocks standing up.
fit_mainsheet_deck_blocks.onThisBoat: One block each side of the middle, with two parts of rope between the boom and each block. From each block the rope runs forward to the foot of the mast, then aft in the covered channel to a clutch. There is no traveller.

fit_self_tacking_track.name: Self-tacking track
fit_self_tacking_track.short: The short rail across the deck in front of the mast for the jib’s car.
fit_self_tacking_track.what: The jib sheet’s car slides along this track. When the boat tacks, the wind pushes the jib across and the car runs to the other end by itself.
fit_self_tacking_track.onThisBoat: Straight, about 2.8 m long, just in front of the mast. Because it is short, the jib cannot be eased far out.
fit_self_tacking_track.showMe: The car sits at the port end of the track, away from the wind. Turn the wind to the other side of the bow in Conditions and watch it slide across.

fit_self_tacking_car.name: Jib car
fit_self_tacking_car.short: The sliding block on the track that the jib sheet runs through.
fit_self_tacking_car.what: The car rides on the self-tacking track and carries the jib sheet’s block. It slides to the side away from the wind by itself.

fit_clutch.name: Rope clutch
fit_clutch.short: A lever that grips a rope so it cannot run out.
fit_clutch.what: A closed clutch holds the rope: it can still be pulled in, but not let out. To let a rope out, take its load on a winch, then open the clutch (lever up).
fit_clutch.onThisBoat: A bank of five clutches in front of each winch, and one single clutch for the jib furling line on the port side deck. In Realistic mode you open and close them with the lever.

mistakes.mistake: Opening a loaded clutch with the rope not on the winch.
mistakes.fix: The rope runs out fast and can burn hands. Put the rope on the winch with a few turns first.

mistakes.mistake: Shutting a clutch on a rope that is running out under load.
mistakes.fix: It can damage the rope. Take the load on the winch first, then close the clutch.

fit_clutch.showMe: Realistic mode: the clutches of this side are the levers in the drawing. Lever up is open; tap a clutch to select it, tap it again to open or close it.

clutch_bank_a.name: Clutch bank A
clutch_bank_a.short: The five clutches on the starboard side.
clutch_bank_a.what: The row of clutches in front of the starboard winch. Each rope from the mast ends at one of them, and any one of them can be put on the winch.
clutch_bank_a.onThisBoat: In order: “Main sheet”, “Main furling” (rolls the main in), “Main furling” (rolls it out), “Main halyard”, “Genoa sheet” (the jib sheet).

clutch_bank_b.name: Clutch bank B
clutch_bank_b.short: The five clutches on the port side.
clutch_bank_b.what: The row of clutches in front of the port winch. Each rope from the mast ends at one of them, and any one of them can be put on the winch.
clutch_bank_b.onThisBoat: In order: “SPI HALYARD” (the gennaker halyard), “Boom lift” (the topping lift), “Main outhaul”, “MAIN SHEET” (the other end of the mainsheet), “Vang”.

clutch_jib_roll.name: Jib furling clutch
clutch_jib_roll.short: The single clutch on the port side deck for the jib furling line.
clutch_jib_roll.what: It holds the jib furling line, so the jib stays rolled up as far as it is.
clutch_jib_roll.onThisBoat: Labelled “JIB ROLL”, beside the sprayhood; from it the line runs aft to the port winch.

fit_rope_bin.name: Rope tail box
fit_rope_bin.short: A box behind each winch where the loose ends of the ropes go.
fit_rope_bin.what: The loose ends (tails) of the ropes go into the box, so the cockpit stays clear and the ropes can run out freely when eased.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving loose rope lying on the cockpit floor.
mistakes.fix: Someone can trip, or the rope tangles as it runs out. Put it in the box.

fit_winch.name: Winch
fit_winch.short: A drum that gives you the power to pull in a heavily loaded rope.
fit_winch.what: The rope is wrapped clockwise round the drum. The turns hold the load (each extra turn multiplies the grip), and turning the drum pulls the rope in. A self-tailer on top grips the tail, so one person can winch alone.
fit_winch.onThisBoat: One electric Lewmar self-tailing winch on each side, worked with a push button; the winch handle is a backup. The winch slows as the load grows and cuts out when the load is too high.

mistakes.mistake: Wrapping the rope anticlockwise.
mistakes.fix: The drum only turns clockwise, so the rope is not held. Wrap it clockwise, seen from above.

mistakes.mistake: Too few turns on a loaded rope.
mistakes.fix: It slips when the clutch opens. Use about 4 turns to winch under load, 2 to ease under control.

mistakes.mistake: Keeping the button pressed when the winch cuts out.
mistakes.fix: The load is too high, often two ropes pulling against each other. Find out why (a closed clutch, the topping lift against the vang) and fix that first.

fit_winch.showMe: Realistic mode, starboard: the jib sheet is on the winch with 2 turns, held by hand. Add turns, put it in the self-tailer, and press the winch button.

winch_primary_port.name: Port winch
winch_primary_port.short: The winch on the left side of the cockpit.
winch_primary_port.what: It works the ropes of clutch bank B and the jib furling line.
winch_primary_port.onThisBoat: Electric, with a self-tailer. The winch handle is kept on this side.

winch_primary_starboard.name: Starboard winch
winch_primary_starboard.short: The winch on the right side of the cockpit.
winch_primary_starboard.what: It works the ropes of clutch bank A.

part_winch_handle.name: Winch handle
part_winch_handle.short: A removable crank for turning a winch, or the furling gearbox at the mast, by hand.
part_winch_handle.what: It fits into the top of a winch. Cranking one way turns the drum fast but weakly (1st gear), the other way slowly but strongly (2nd gear); the drum turns the same way both times.
part_winch_handle.onThisBoat: One handle on board, kept at the port side. It is used mostly at the mast, to roll the main in by hand if the furling line slips. While you carry it, your hands are full.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving the handle in the winch after use.
mistakes.fix: It can whip round or fall overboard. Take it out and put it back in its place.

mistakes.mistake: Cranking in 1st gear against a heavy load.
mistakes.fix: It hardly moves. Crank the other way (2nd gear).

part_winch_handle.showMe: Realistic mode, Port station: the winch handle sits in its slot. Tap the handle to pick it up.

winch_secondary_port.name: Port secondary winch (optional)
winch_secondary_port.short: A second winch some boats have on the left side; not on this boat.
winch_secondary_port.what: The builder offers a second winch on each side, so more ropes can be worked at once. The reference boat does not have them, so the app does not draw them.

winch_secondary_starboard.name: Starboard secondary winch (optional)
winch_secondary_starboard.short: A second winch some boats have on the right side; not on this boat.
winch_secondary_starboard.what: The builder offers a second winch on each side, so more ropes can be worked at once. The reference boat does not have them, so the app does not draw them.

helm_port.name: Port wheel
helm_port.short: The steering wheel on the left side.
helm_port.what: Either wheel turns the same rudder. Steering from the side lets you see past the sails.
helm_port.onThisBoat: Twin wheels, each with a compass in front of it.

helm_starboard.name: Starboard wheel
helm_starboard.short: The steering wheel on the right side.
helm_starboard.what: Either wheel turns the same rudder. Steering from the side lets you see past the sails.
helm_starboard.onThisBoat: Twin wheels, each with a compass in front of it.

fit_compass.name: Compass
fit_compass.short: Shows which way the boat is heading.
fit_compass.what: The compass shows the boat’s heading in degrees: 0 north, 90 east, 180 south, 270 west.
fit_compass.onThisBoat: One compass in front of each wheel.

engine_control.name: Engine control lever
engine_control.short: One lever for both the gear and the throttle.
engine_control.what: Pushed forward from the middle, the lever puts the engine in ahead gear, then gives more power; pulled back, astern. In the middle the engine is in neutral. Pause in neutral when you change direction.
engine_control.onThisBoat: An Allpa single-lever control with START, STOP and POWER buttons and a “MAX 2500 RPM” sticker. In the app the lever two-thirds ahead gives about 1,850 rpm and 8 kn; full ahead about 9.3 kn.

mistakes.mistake: Moving the lever from ahead straight to astern.
mistakes.fix: The gearbox suffers. Stop in neutral for a moment, then go astern.

mistakes.mistake: Starting the engine with the lever in gear.
mistakes.fix: She moves off at once. Put the lever in neutral before you start.

engine_control.showMe: No wind, engine running with the lever two-thirds ahead: about 1,850 rpm and 8 kn. The Engine section has the lever.

term_sheet.name: Sheet
term_sheet.short: A rope that sets a sail’s angle to the wind.
term_sheet.what: A sheet pulls on a sail’s clew (its back bottom corner) and so sets how far the sail can swing out. Each sail has its own: the mainsheet and the jib sheet. On a boat a sheet is a rope, not the sail.

term_halyard.name: Halyard
term_halyard.short: A rope that hoists a sail.
term_halyard.what: A halyard pulls a sail’s head (its top corner) up the mast or the forestay and holds it there.
term_halyard.onThisBoat: The main stays hoisted and rolls into the mast, and the jib rolls round the forestay, so the halyards are hardly ever touched; the gennaker halyard is parked.

term_port.name: Port

alternatives.note: an old word, no longer used

term_port.short: The left side of the boat, looking forward.
term_port.what: Port is the left side when you face the bow, whichever way you stand. Its navigation light is red.

mistakes.mistake: Saying “left” while facing the stern.
mistakes.fix: Port never changes: it is always the left side looking forward. Use port and starboard on board.

term_starboard.name: Starboard
term_starboard.short: The right side of the boat, looking forward.
term_starboard.what: Starboard is the right side when you face the bow. Its navigation light is green.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing up port and starboard in a hurry.
mistakes.fix: A memory aid: “port” and “left” both have four letters.

term_windward.name: Windward
term_windward.short: The side the wind comes from.
term_windward.what: The windward side of the boat is the side the wind blows onto. Windward also means towards the wind.
term_windward.showMe: Wind from starboard: starboard is the windward side, and the boom has swung out to port, the leeward side.

term_leeward.name: Leeward
term_leeward.short: The side away from the wind.
term_leeward.what: Leeward (sailors say “loo-ard”) is the side the wind blows away from. The sails and the boom lie on the leeward side, and the boat heels towards it.
term_leeward.showMe: Wind from starboard: the boom and the sails lie to port, the leeward side.

term_true_wind.name: True wind
term_true_wind.short: The wind as it blows over the water, as a boat standing still feels it.
term_true_wind.what: The true wind is the wind’s own direction and speed over the water. Conditions sets it, and the instruments show it as TWA and TWS.
term_true_wind.showMe: The map shows the true wind and, while she sails, the apparent wind she feels.

term_apparent_wind.name: Apparent wind
term_apparent_wind.short: The wind the boat feels: the true wind plus the wind from her own speed.
term_apparent_wind.what: When the boat moves, her own speed adds a headwind. Together with the true wind it makes the apparent wind, which is what the sails feel and the masthead arrow shows. Sailing towards the wind or across it, the apparent wind comes from further ahead than the true wind and is stronger; running away from it, it is weaker.

mistakes.mistake: Trimming the sails to the true wind.
mistakes.fix: The sails feel the apparent wind, which comes from further ahead when she moves. Trim to the telltales and the masthead arrow.

term_apparent_wind.showMe: Sailing with the wind from the side: the map shows the apparent wind coming from further ahead than the true wind.

term_starboard_tack.name: Starboard tack
term_starboard_tack.short: Sailing with the wind coming over the starboard side.
term_starboard_tack.what: On starboard tack the wind comes from the starboard side, and the boom and the sails are out to port.
term_starboard_tack.showMe: Wind from starboard, boom out to port: she is on starboard tack.

term_port_tack.name: Port tack
term_port_tack.short: Sailing with the wind coming over the port side.
term_port_tack.what: On port tack the wind comes from the port side, and the boom and the sails are out to starboard.
term_port_tack.showMe: Wind from port, boom out to starboard: she is on port tack.

term_tacking.name: Tacking
term_tacking.short: Turning the bow through the wind to the other side.
term_tacking.what: To tack, the boat turns towards the wind, through the no-go zone and on until the wind comes over the other side. With a self-tacking jib only the wheel is needed: the jib and the main swing across by themselves.

mistakes.mistake: Turning too slowly.
mistakes.fix: She stops head to wind (in irons). Turn steadily and keep her moving.

term_tacking.showMe: Close-hauled, the autopilot holding the wind angle: press “Tack” in the Autopilot section and watch the bow turn through the wind and the jib cross by itself.

term_gybe.name: Gybe
term_gybe.short: Turning the stern through the wind, so the boom crosses to the other side.
term_gybe.what: In a gybe the stern turns through the wind and the boom swings across the whole boat. Done on purpose, the mainsheet is hauled in first so the boom crosses a short way, under control. By accident (an accidental gybe) it crosses fast and hard: it can injure people and break gear.

mistakes.mistake: Gybing with the mainsheet eased right out.
mistakes.fix: The boom slams across. Haul the mainsheet in before turning, then ease it out on the new side.

mistakes.mistake: Steering too far downwind.
mistakes.fix: The wind gets behind the main and it can gybe by itself. Stay a little off dead downwind.

term_gybe.showMe: The autopilot turns her through dead downwind with the mainsheet eased: the boom crosses fast (an accidental gybe) and the red area shows its path. In a controlled gybe the mainsheet is hauled in first.

term_luffing.name: Luffing (sail flapping)
term_luffing.short: A sail flapping at its front edge because it is let out too far.
term_luffing.what: When a sail is eased more than the wind angle needs, or the boat turns too close to the wind, the air reaches both sides of the front edge and the sail flaps. It no longer drives the boat, and long flapping in strong wind wears it out.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving a sail flapping in strong wind.
mistakes.fix: It wears and can tear. Haul it in, or roll it away.

term_luffing.showMe: The mainsheet is eased right out: the mainsail flaps along its front edge. Haul the mainsheet in (Ropes section) until the flapping just stops.

term_ease.name: Ease
term_ease.what: Easing lets a rope out slowly and under control, so a sail can go further out or a load comes off.

term_trim.name: Trim / haul in
term_trim.short: To pull a rope in; also, setting the sails to the wind.
term_trim.what: Hauling in pulls a rope in. Trimming means setting each sail to the wind: haul in until it stops flapping, ease until it is not stalled.

term_twist.name: Twist
term_twist.short: How much the top of a sail opens out compared with its bottom.
term_twist.what: With twist, the top of the sail stands further out than the bottom. A little twist is normal; more twist spills power, which helps in strong wind. The vang controls it on the mainsail, the sheet on the jib.
term_twist.showMe: The vang is eased all the way: the top of the mainsail twists open. Haul the vang (Ropes section) and the twist closes.

term_telltale.name: Telltales
term_telltale.short: Ribbons on the sails that show how the air flows.
term_telltale.what: Telltales are short ribbons near the front of the sails. Both sides streaming straight back: good trim. The far side drooping: pulled in too far. The near side lifting: let out too far.
term_telltale.showMe: Good trim: zoom in on the front of the mainsail; the telltales on both sides stream straight back.

part_telltale.name: Telltale
part_telltale.short: A short ribbon on a sail that shows how the air flows over it.
part_telltale.what: Telltales are short ribbons near the front of a sail, one on each side. Both streaming straight back: the sail is trimmed well. The one on the side away from the wind drooping or spinning: the sail is pulled in too far. The one on the wind’s side lifting: it is let out too far.
part_telltale.onThisBoat: The app draws telltales near the front edge of both sails.

mistakes.mistake: Hauling in until the sail stops flapping, then hauling more “to be safe”.
mistakes.fix: The telltales on the far side droop: the sail has stalled. Ease until both sides stream.

part_telltale.showMe: Good trim: zoom in (pinch) on the front edge of the mainsail near the mast. The telltales on both sides stream straight back.

term_no_go_zone.name: No-go zone
term_no_go_zone.short: The directions, about 45° either side of the wind, a sailing boat cannot sail in.
term_no_go_zone.what: No sailing boat can sail straight into the wind. Within about 45° of it (30–50°, depending on the boat) the sails flap and she slows to a stop. To get upwind she zigzags, tacking from one side to the other.

mistakes.mistake: Steering into the no-go zone.
mistakes.fix: The sails flap and she stops. Turn away from the wind until the sails fill.

term_no_go_zone.showMe: The map shows the no-go zone as a wedge towards the wind. She is sailing just outside it, close-hauled.

term_close_hauled.name: Close-hauled
term_close_hauled.short: Sailing as close to the wind as she can, about 45° off it.
term_close_hauled.what: Close-hauled, the sails are pulled in tight and the boat sails as near to the wind as she can, just outside the no-go zone. She heels most on this point of sail.
term_close_hauled.showMe: Close-hauled: the wind 45° off the bow, both sails pulled in; she heels about 17°.

term_close_reach.name: Close reach
term_close_reach.short: Sailing with the wind about 60° off the bow, between close-hauled and a beam reach.
term_close_reach.what: On a close reach the sails are eased a little from close-hauled. She sails fast and still heels well.
term_close_reach.showMe: Close reach: the wind 60° off the bow, the sails eased a little; she sails at about 7.5 kn.

term_beam_reach.name: Beam reach
term_beam_reach.short: Sailing with the wind at right angles to the boat.
term_beam_reach.what: On a beam reach the wind comes from the side, 90° off the bow, and the sails are eased about halfway. For many boats it is the fastest point of sail.
term_beam_reach.showMe: Beam reach: the wind from the side, the sails eased about halfway; she sails at about 8 kn.

term_broad_reach.name: Broad reach
term_broad_reach.short: Sailing with the wind from behind the side, about 135° off the bow.
term_broad_reach.what: On a broad reach the wind comes over the back corner of the boat. The sails are eased well out; she heels little and the ride is easy.
term_broad_reach.showMe: Broad reach: the wind 135° off the bow, the sails eased right out; she hardly heels.

term_run.name: Running
term_run.short: Sailing with the wind from behind.
term_run.what: Running, the wind comes from (almost) straight behind and the sails are eased right out. She is slower than on a reach, and the boom can gybe across if the wind gets behind the mainsail.

mistakes.mistake: Running dead downwind.
mistakes.fix: The boom can gybe by accident. Steer a little off dead downwind, so the wind stays clearly on one side.

term_run.showMe: Running: the wind from almost straight behind, the sails right out; about 4.7 kn, slower than on a reach.

term_reef.name: Reefing
term_reef.short: Making a sail smaller for strong wind.
term_reef.what: Reefing makes the sails smaller, so the boat heels less and is easier to control in strong wind. Reef early, before the wind is strong.
term_reef.onThisBoat: There are no reef lines: the main is made smaller by rolling part of it into the mast, and the jib by rolling part of it round the forestay; usually the jib first, then the main.

mistakes.mistake: Waiting until the wind is already strong.
mistakes.fix: Rolling sail away is harder and riskier under load. Make the sails smaller as soon as she heels too much.

term_reef.showMe: The mainsail is rolled halfway into the mast: half the sail, less push.

term_preventer.name: Preventer
term_preventer.short: A line that holds the boom out so it cannot gybe across.
term_preventer.what: A preventer runs from the end of the boom forward and back to the cockpit, holding the boom out when running, so it cannot swing across in an accidental gybe.
term_preventer.onThisBoat: This boat carries none, so the app teaches the controlled gybe: the mainsheet hauled in first.

term_north.name: North
term_north.what: North is 0° (or 360°) on the compass; east is 90°, south 180°, west 270°. Winds are named for where they come from, so a north wind blows from the north.

term_east.name: East
term_east.what: East is 90° on the compass, where the sun rises. An east wind blows from the east.

term_south.name: South
term_south.what: South is 180° on the compass. A south wind blows from the south.

term_west.name: West
term_west.what: West is 270° on the compass, where the sun sets. A west wind blows from the west.

term_compass_point.name: Compass point
term_compass_point.short: One of the 32 named directions of the compass, 11¼° apart.
term_compass_point.what: Before degrees, sailors named 32 directions: north, east, south and west, the four between them (north-east, south-east, south-west, north-west), and more between those. One point is 11¼°, so “two points off the bow” is about 22° to one side of straight ahead.

term_ahead.name: Ahead
term_ahead.what: Ahead means in the direction the bow points; “dead ahead” is straight in front. With the engine, going ahead means moving forwards.

term_astern.name: Astern
term_astern.short: Behind the boat; also, moving backwards.
term_astern.what: Astern means behind the stern. With the engine, going astern means moving backwards (reverse gear).

term_abeam.name: Abeam
term_abeam.short: At right angles to the boat, straight out to one side.
term_abeam.what: Something abeam is at 90° to the boat’s centreline, level with her middle, to port or to starboard. A wind from abeam makes a beam reach.

term_quarter.name: Quarter
term_quarter.short: The back corners of the boat, between abeam and astern.
term_quarter.what: The quarters are the back corners of the boat. Wind or waves “on the quarter” come from behind at an angle, about 135° off the bow; waves from there are the hardest to steer in.
term_quarter.showMe: Wind and waves on the starboard quarter: watch the wheel (the autopilot) keep correcting as the waves push her off course.

term_heading.name: Heading

alternatives.note: strictly, the direction she moves over the ground

term_heading.short: The compass direction the bow points.
term_heading.what: The heading is the direction the bow points, in degrees from north: 0 north, 90 east, 180 south, 270 west. The autopilot’s Heading mode holds it.
term_heading.showMe: The map shows her heading 060°, towards the north-east, with the wind from the side.

term_wind_direction.name: Wind direction
term_wind_direction.short: Where the wind comes from, in degrees or compass names.
term_wind_direction.what: A wind is named for where it comes from: a north wind (a northerly) blows from the north towards the south. In degrees, a wind “from 060°” comes from the north-east.

mistakes.mistake: Reading a wind “from 060°” as blowing towards 060°.
mistakes.fix: It blows from 060° towards 240°: look towards 060° to face it.

term_wind_direction.showMe: Wind from 060° (north-east): the streaks blow from there across the boat.

term_knot.name: Knot
term_knot.short: One nautical mile per hour: how speed is measured at sea.
term_knot.what: Boat and wind speeds at sea are given in knots. One knot is one nautical mile (1,852 m) per hour, about 0.5 m/s or 1.85 km/h.

term_beaufort.name: Beaufort scale
term_beaufort.short: Wind strength as a number from 0 to 12, judged by its effect on the sea.
term_beaufort.what: The Beaufort scale names wind strengths from 0 (calm) to 12 (hurricane). Force 3 (7–10 kn) brings the first scattered white horses; force 4 (11–16 kn) fairly frequent ones; force 5 (17–21 kn) many.
term_beaufort.showMe: 10 kn, the top of force 3: the first scattered white horses. Raise the wind in Conditions to see more.

term_gust.name: Gust
term_gust.short: A sudden, short increase in the wind.
term_gust.what: A gust is a burst of stronger wind lasting seconds, often from a slightly different direction. It can show on the water as a darker, rougher patch coming towards you. In a gust the boat heels more.

mistakes.mistake: Holding the mainsheet tight through a strong gust.
mistakes.fix: She heels hard and turns into the wind. Ease the main as the gust hits, and trim again when it has passed.

term_gust.showMe: Gusty wind: watch upwind for a dark patch on the water. When it arrives, the strip shows GUST and she heels more.

term_lull.name: Lull
term_lull.short: A short drop in the wind.
term_lull.what: A lull is a moment of weaker wind, often between gusts. The boat stands up and slows down, and the wind the sails feel comes from a little further ahead.

term_wind_shift.name: Wind shift
term_wind_shift.short: A change in the wind’s direction.
term_wind_shift.what: The wind’s direction keeps changing a little. A shift that comes from further ahead is a header: she has to bear away, or the sails flap. One from further behind is a lift: she can point closer to the wind.
term_wind_shift.showMe: Shifty wind with the autopilot holding the wind angle: watch her heading swing as the wind shifts.

term_bora.name: Bora

alternatives.note: the Croatian name, also used by sailors there

term_bora.short: A cold, very gusty wind from the north-east in the Adriatic.
term_bora.what: The bora blows from the north to north-east, down from the mountains onto the Adriatic coast, most often in winter. It comes in sudden, strong gusts and raises short, high waves with white crests.

term_jugo.name: Jugo

alternatives.note: the Italian name for the same kind of wind

term_jugo.short: A warm, humid wind from the south-east in the Adriatic.
term_jugo.what: The jugo blows from the south-east, warm and moist, and can bring rain and storms. Its name means “southern” in Croatian.

term_maestral.name: Maestral
term_maestral.short: The summer sea breeze from the north-west on the Adriatic coast.
term_maestral.what: On summer days, when the coast gets warmer than the sea, a mild wind blows in from the sea from the north-west: the maestral.

term_heel.name: Heel
term_heel.short: The boat leaning over to one side.
term_heel.what: The wind’s push on the sails tips the boat over to leeward; the keel’s weight pulls her back. Some heel is normal; too much slows her and makes her hard to steer. Easing the sheets or making the sails smaller reduces it.

mistakes.mistake: Hauling the sheets in harder when she heels too much.
mistakes.fix: That makes more heel. Ease the mainsheet, or roll part of the sails in.

term_heel.showMe: 20 kn with the sails pulled in: she heels about 30°. Ease the mainsheet in the Ropes section and she stands up.

term_weather_helm.name: Weather helm
term_weather_helm.short: The boat’s pull to turn into the wind, felt on the wheel.
term_weather_helm.what: A heeling boat wants to turn her bow into the wind. To keep a straight course, the wheel must be held turned away from the wind. A little is normal; a lot means too much heel or too much mainsail: ease the main.
term_weather_helm.showMe: Heeled hard in 20 kn: the autopilot holds the wheel turned away from the wind to keep her straight. Ease the mainsheet and the wheel comes back towards the middle.

term_round_up.name: Round-up

alternatives.note: a violent round-up, often with waves from behind

term_round_up.short: The boat turning into the wind by herself, and the wheel cannot stop her.
term_round_up.what: Overpowered in a gust, the boat heels, the rudder loses its grip and she swings up into the wind with the sails flapping. Easing the mainsheet early stops it.

mistakes.mistake: Fighting it with the wheel alone.
mistakes.fix: A rudder turned hard over stops gripping. Ease the mainsheet: that takes away the force that turns her.

term_in_irons.name: In irons
term_in_irons.short: Stopped head to wind, with no steering.
term_in_irons.what: Turned straight into the wind, the boat loses her drive: the sails flap, she slows and stops, and with no water flowing past the rudder the wheel does nothing. To get out, let her drift backwards with the wheel turned until the bow falls off the wind, or use the engine.
term_in_irons.showMe: Heading straight into the wind at 6 kn: the sails flap, she slows down and stops, and the wheel no longer turns her.

term_head_up.name: Head up
term_head_up.short: To turn the bow towards the wind.
term_head_up.what: Heading up turns the bow closer to the wind; the sails then need hauling in, or they flap. The opposite is bearing away.

term_bear_away.name: Bear away
term_bear_away.short: To turn the bow away from the wind.
term_bear_away.what: Bearing away turns the bow further from the wind; the sails then need easing out. Bearing away too far with the wind behind risks an accidental gybe.

term_stall.name: Stall
term_stall.short: A sail pulled in too far, so the air no longer flows smoothly round it.
term_stall.what: A stalled sail looks full but drives poorly and makes more heel; the telltales on its far side droop or spin. Ease the sheet until they stream.
term_stall.showMe: The mainsheet is hauled right in with the wind 60° off the bow: the main is stalled. Ease it to about 25 % in the Ropes section and she speeds up.

term_hull_speed.name: Hull speed
term_hull_speed.short: The speed a heavy boat can hardly go beyond: about 9 kn for this one.
term_hull_speed.what: A heavy boat pushes a wave along with her. Near about 1.34 × √(waterline length in feet) knots she sits in that wave, and more power hardly makes her faster. For this boat that is about 8.9 kn.
term_hull_speed.showMe: Full throttle, no wind: 2,500 rpm gives about 9.3 kn. With a third less throttle she still makes about 8 kn: the last of the power adds little speed.

term_fetch.name: Fetch
term_fetch.short: How far the wind has blown over open water to reach you.
term_fetch.what: The longer the fetch and the stronger the wind, the bigger the waves. In a sheltered bay the fetch is short and the sea stays small; in the open sea it is long.
term_fetch.showMe: Sheltered water in 15 kn: small waves. Set “Waves” in Conditions to “Open sea”: the same wind makes much bigger waves.

term_white_horses.name: White horses
term_white_horses.short: Breaking wave crests that show white.
term_white_horses.what: When the wind reaches about 7–10 kn (force 3), the first wave crests break into white foam; the stronger the wind, the more of them.
term_white_horses.showMe: 22 kn in the open sea: white horses everywhere. At 6 kn there are none.

term_wave_height.name: Wave height
term_wave_height.short: How high the bigger waves are, from trough to crest.
term_wave_height.what: The wave height given in forecasts is the average of the highest third of the waves; single waves can be almost twice as high. The Waves block in Conditions shows it.
term_wave_height.showMe: Coastal waves in 15 kn: the Waves block in Conditions says they are 0.7 m high, one every 3.8 s.

term_heave.name: Heave
term_heave.short: The boat rising and falling on the waves.
term_heave.what: Heave is the up-and-down motion as the waves pass under the boat.
term_heave.showMe: Open sea in 20 kn, the boat held still: she rises and falls by about 0.9 m each way.

term_pitch.name: Pitch
term_pitch.short: The bow rising and falling as the waves pass.
term_pitch.what: Pitch is the boat tipping nose up and nose down. Waves from ahead or from behind make her pitch most.
term_pitch.showMe: Waves from ahead: she pitches, bow up and down, by about 3°.

term_roll.name: Roll
term_roll.short: The boat rocking from side to side.
term_roll.what: Roll is the boat tipping from side to side. Waves from the side make her roll most.
term_roll.showMe: Waves from the side: she rolls by about 5° each way.

part_vang_strut.name: Rigid vang strut
part_vang_strut.short: A spring-loaded strut under the boom that holds it up; the vang rope pulls it down.
part_vang_strut.what: A rigid vang is a strut from low on the mast to the underside of the boom, with a spring inside. The spring pushes the boom up; the vang’s rope tackle pulls it down. With it, the boom does not drop when the sail is rolled away.
part_vang_strut.onThisBoat: A Seldén Rodkicker with a gas spring.

fit_mast_base_turning_blocks.name: Turning blocks at the mast foot
fit_mast_base_turning_blocks.short: The ring of pulleys at the foot of the mast that turn the ropes aft.
fit_mast_base_turning_blocks.what: Ropes come down the mast and turn at these blocks to run aft along the coachroof to the cockpit, so they can be worked from there.
fit_mast_base_turning_blocks.onThisBoat: Seldén blocks in a ring round the foot of the mast, one block for each rope.

fit_line_channels.name: Line channels
fit_line_channels.short: Covered channels on the coachroof that carry the ropes to the cockpit.
fit_line_channels.what: They keep the ropes from the mast tidy and out from under the crew’s feet on their way aft.
fit_line_channels.onThisBoat: One channel on each side, ending at the clutch banks in front of the winches.

fit_sprayhood.name: Sprayhood
fit_sprayhood.short: The folding canvas shelter at the front of the cockpit.
fit_sprayhood.what: The sprayhood shields the companionway and the front of the cockpit from spray and wind. It folds down when it is not needed.

fit_anchor_windlass.name: Anchor windlass
fit_anchor_windlass.short: The electric winch on the bow that lets the anchor chain out and pulls it in.
fit_anchor_windlass.what: The windlass lowers the anchor and hauls it back up, worked by switches at the bow or a remote at the helm.
fit_anchor_windlass.onThisBoat: On the foredeck behind the anchor roller. The app does not draw it yet; anchoring comes in a later phase.

mistakes.mistake: Putting fingers or feet near the chain while the windlass runs.
mistakes.fix: The chain can trap them. Keep clear, and stop the windlass before you touch the chain.

fit_bow_roller.name: Bow roller
fit_bow_roller.short: The roller at the bow that the anchor chain runs over.
fit_bow_roller.what: The anchor sits in the bow roller, and its chain runs over it to the windlass.

fit_mooring_cleat.name: Mooring cleat
fit_mooring_cleat.short: A strong fitting for tying the mooring lines to.
fit_mooring_cleat.what: Lines to a pier or a buoy are made fast round a cleat.
fit_mooring_cleat.onThisBoat: Cleats at the bow (photo). The app does not draw them yet.

env_wake.name: Wake
env_wake.short: The trail of stirred-up water the boat leaves behind her.
env_wake.what: The wake is the trail of water stirred up behind the boat as she moves. A straight wake means a steady course; a curved one shows she has been turning.
env_wake.showMe: Sailing fast with the wind from the side: the wake trails out behind her. Turn the wheel a little to see it curve.

env_boom_danger_zone.name: Boom danger zone
env_boom_danger_zone.short: The red area the app draws where the boom would sweep in a gybe.
env_boom_danger_zone.what: With the wind from behind, the boom can swing across the whole cockpit in an accidental gybe, fast and hard enough to injure someone. The app draws the area it would sweep in red, so you know where not to stand.

mistakes.mistake: Steering so far downwind that the wind gets behind the mainsail (sailing by the lee).
mistakes.fix: The boom can cross at any moment. Steer a little back towards the wind, or gybe on purpose with the mainsheet hauled in.

env_boom_danger_zone.showMe: Running, the autopilot turns her through dead downwind with the mainsheet eased: an accidental gybe. The red area shows where the boom sweeps across. Keep heads out of it.

env_buoy.name: Practice buoy
env_buoy.short: One of four yellow buoys near the start, to sail round.
env_buoy.what: Four yellow buoys stand 200 m north, east, south and west of where the boat starts. Use them as marks: sail round them, or check how far you have gone.
env_buoy.showMe: The map from above: zoom out with − four times to see the four buoys round the start.

fit_autopilot_control.name: Autopilot control
fit_autopilot_control.short: The control panel that lets the autopilot steer.
fit_autopilot_control.what: The autopilot steers for you. On Standby you steer; Heading holds the compass course; Wind holds the angle to the true wind. Tack turns the boat through the wind.
fit_autopilot_control.onThisBoat: A B&G control at the helm. The Autopilot section is the app’s version of it.

mistakes.mistake: Holding a compass heading and forgetting the wind.
mistakes.fix: If the wind shifts, she can end up in the no-go zone or gybe. Watch the sails, or let the autopilot hold the wind angle.

mistakes.mistake: Turning the wheel by hand with the autopilot on.
mistakes.fix: It goes to Standby (you took the wheel). Choose a mode again when you want it to steer.

fit_autopilot_control.showMe: The autopilot is holding the angle to the wind. Its section is called Autopilot: change the angle with its buttons.

fit_instrument_display.name: Instrument display
fit_instrument_display.short: The screen at the helm that shows speed, heading and the wind.
fit_instrument_display.what: It shows the boat’s speed, her heading and the wind: AWA and AWS, the apparent wind’s angle and speed (what the sails feel), and TWA and TWS, the true wind’s.
fit_instrument_display.onThisBoat: A B&G display at the helm. In the app, the strip at the top of the 3D view shows the same numbers; tap it for the wind dial.
